canberra.title: Stephen-Smith Deputy Chief Minister in reset for Barr Government
canberra.snippet: The ACT’s new deputy Chief Minister is Rachel Stephen-Smith, while the new minister in cabinet is Caitlin Tough from the southern s...
canberra.content:
New Deputy Chief Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith, Chief Minister Andrew Barr and new minister Caitlin Tough. Photo: ACT Government.

The ACT’s new deputy Chief Minister is Rachel Stephen-Smith, while the new minister in cabinet is Caitlin Tough from the southern seat of Brindabella, in what Labor hopes will be a reset for the government after the tumultuous events of last week.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr announced the new Labor ministry after a caucus meeting on Monday (27 July) necessitated by the resignation of former Deputy Chief Minister Yvette Berry last Thursday after the tabling of the Operation Kingfisher report from the ACT Integrity Commission.

The appointments of Ms Stephen-Smith and Ms Tough were no surprise, with caucus in unanimous agreement.

But the shuffling of portfolios brought significant changes for the government and the renaming of some portfolio areas.

Ms Stephen-Smith will hand over Health and Mental Health to Marisa Paterson while retaining responsibility for Health Infrastructure, in particular the Northside Hospital project.

She will take on the key Education portfolio where there are significant resourcing challenges, industrial strife and the Strong Foundations reform program to roll out.

Chris Steel has relinquished Transport to Attorney-General and City Services Minister Tara Cheyne, which some may see as a demotion, but he retains carriage of light rail, and picks up Sport and Recreation. He will stay Planning and Sustainable Development Minister.

Dr Paterson will retain Police, Fire and Emergency Services and Gaming Reform but lose Women to Ms Tough.

Suzanne Orr will take on another of Ms Berry’s key portfolios, Housing and Homelessness, but community services, veterans and seniors will go to Ms Tough, who will tackle one of the government’s most challenging areas, Corrections, as well as Human Rights.

Michael Pettersson will combine Night-Time Economy with Arts and Creative Industries, while retaining Skills, Training and Industrial Relations, Multicultural Affairs, and Children, Youth and Families.

Mr Barr will have an overarching role as Minister for Major Projects; trade will now sit with a new portfolio of Trade, Investment and the Knowledge Economy, and he will oversee a new Tourism and Events portfolio.

Mr Barr said last week’s events presented the government with an opportunity for renewal.

He said the new cabinet was a strong team that had representatives from each electorate and combined experience with fresh perspectives.

“It’s been structured around the priorities that matter most to Canberrans,” he said.

Mr Barr rejected suggestions that he was simply rearranging the deckchairs.

He said Labor remained the party with the greatest support in the community, and it had acknowledged and apologised for its mistakes in government.

“No one is perfect,” he said. “But what I can say is that this team is committed to delivering on the things we took to the election, and working as constructively as we can with a very diverse parliament in a very fractured political environment to achieve as much as we can for Canberrans.”

New minister Caitlin Tough is excited and nervous about her new challenges. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Ms Stephen-Smith’s ascension cements her favouritism to succeed Mr Barr as Chief Minister, but she said her focus was on her new roles.

“I’ve got big new portfolios in education and child development and wellbeing – that’s going to be a steep learning curve,” she said.

Ms Stephen-Smith said she would be contacting the teachers union and Education Directorate to seek a resolution of the current dispute, and building on the reform platform that Ms Berry had laid for the ACT’s public schools.

“My aim is not to throw all the cards up in the air, but back in that reform for the future, work with children and young people, families, teachers, unions and other stakeholders to ensure that we’re delivering on the very clear plan that’s been laid out by Yvette as the Education Minister,” she said.

Ms Stephen-Smith said it was important to hang on to health infrastructure at such a critical point for the Northside Hospital project, which was heading towards the end of the very early contractor involvement stage.

She felt she was leaving Health in a better place after years of reform, with more to come, that was making inroads into some of the sector’s ongoing issues such as elective surgery wait lists and emergency department response time.

Mr Barr said continuity was also behind Mr Steel keeping light rail, which was also intrinsic to planning for the Southern Gateway. When light rail stage 2B moved to the delivery stage, Infrastructure Canberra would take over.

He rejected the view that losing Transport was a demotion for Mr Steel, who had to wear a Legislative Assembly censure for the MyWay+ ticketing debacle.

“He was clear that he had some big priorities he wanted to pursue in planning and wanted to take on a new portfolio opportunity,” Mr Barr said.

“Sport and Recreation is one of the most reported areas. It’s one he’s very passionate about, and has actually asked to do it before, and so now he gets that opportunity.”

Ms Tough said she was excited, nervous and a bit sad given the circumstances of her move to cabinet.

She said the reallocation of portfolios was a really important rebalancing of cabinet to have someone from Brindabella back at the table and have the voice of Tuggeranong back in the room where decisions were being made.

“I plan to really stand up for my community of Tuggeranong in the cabinet room, and make sure everyone’s voice is heard,” she said.

The Corrections role has defeated others, but Ms Tough said she was looking forward to “delving in deep” and understanding what’s going on in that portfolio much more than as a backbencher.

“I’m someone who likes to put my head down and get the work done, so I’m really looking forward to the opportunity to tackle what’s going on there and see what we can do next,” she said.

Mr Barr was asked about increasing the size of the assembly to expand the talent pool but said now was not the time and the public had no appetite for more MLAs.

The new cabinet is:

Chief Minister

Minister for Trade, Investment and the Knowledge Economy
Minister for Tourism and Events

canberra.title: A community search and a $950 ‘reward’ helps Canberra woman reunite with invaluable bike
canberra.snippet: The victim of a midnight theft has thanked the Canberra community for helping her reunite with the invaluable bike that she relies on to ...
canberra.content:
Peta Raftopolous was shocked to find that her custom-made electric bike was stolen last Thursday. After a few days of spreading the news, she finally has it back, but it came at a price. Photo: Peta Raftopolous.

The victim of a midnight theft has thanked the Canberra community for helping her reunite with the invaluable bike that she relies on to transport her family.

Mother of two, Peta Raftopolous, lives with dwarfism and uses her custom-made electric bike to help her effectively travel across the city.

On Thursday 23 July, Peta woke up to find that her precious vehicle had been stolen. In an effort to get it back, Peta took to social media, calling on nearby residents to keep an eye out.

After being blown away by the response of her neighbours and their offerings of support, Peta was reunited with her bike on Monday (27 July), but it came at a cost. $950 to be exact.

“Between midnight and early morning, I woke up to find my courtyard gates wide open, and my bike and its trailer both missing,” she said.

“As soon as I realised, I put the kids in front of the TV and just started scanning notice boards with photos of my bike while trying to explain why it has no resale value for anyone who had stolen it.

“I then spent the next two days putting posters up with money offerings for anyone who returned it.

“In that time, I had so many people reach out offering to look in certain areas, telling me their stories about bike thefts and even at one point someone offered to start a GoFundMe, which I politely declined.”

While nothing came of the wide public search for Peta’s bike, it was a Sunday evening phone call that saw her reunited with her bike once more.

“I got phone calls from a private number saying that she had been sold my bike, which she bought for her son for $800,” she said.

“She said she’d give it back to me for $1000. It was quite clearly either the person who stole it or someone very closely affiliated.

“She had this whole story, so I said, ‘OK, then I’ll give you the $800 for it.’ She was like, ‘Oh no, I want an extra $150 for the inconvenience’.”

Despite now being $950 out of pocket, Peta thanked the community at large for their support.

“I feel really supported, and I did not feel alone, which was really nice,” she said.

“It was great to see the community really rally around something like this. They saw how reliant I am on my custom-made bike, and it wasn’t as easy as just buying a new one.”

Peta explained it is quite difficult for people with dwarfism to have things made for their size and that it is rare to find things like bikes, prams and seats that properly cater for their needs.

“My biggest concern about losing my bike initially was that I wouldn’t be able to get one like it again,” she said.

“Making custom-sized products like the bike I’ve got, although it costs thousands of dollars, isn’t profitable for manufacturers to make.

“When I see things like prams, for example, you’ve got to buy multiple because it’s really unlikely that they will go on sale again. The pram I have, I bought four of them because there was no chance that if mine broke, I’d be able to get one similar again.”

Despite the stressful few days, Peta said she is glad to have her bike back.

“Travelling with the electric bike is so much easier for my kids and me,” she said.

“While I can drive a car, it is difficult for me to get my kids in and out of it. Using the electric bike, it’s not just better for me but for my kids as well.

“It’s better for them not to have a stressed mum.”

canberra.title: Teenage trio charged over alleged arson attack that left residents with minor injuries
canberra.snippet: Three teenagers have faced court after allegedly setting a Giralang home alight before attempting to escape interstate. Emergency service...
canberra.content:
27 July 2026

The trio, aged 17 or 18, have been extradited to Canberra after allegedly using jerry-cans of fuel to attack a Giralang home. Photos: ACT Policing.

Three teenagers have faced court after allegedly setting a Giralang home alight before attempting to escape interstate.

Emergency services were called to a house fire in Gidjili Place in Giralang at about 11:10 am on Friday (24 July),

In a statement, an ACT Policing spokesperson said jerry-cans of fuel were poured throughout the home before it was set alight.

The two female residents of the home, who received minor injuries during the incident, claimed two males had entered the home.

“Multiple police resources responded, with officers and intelligence staff quickly able to establish via witness reports and CCTV review that the two males allegedly responsible for the fire had fled the area in a silver Audi sedan driven by a third male,” they said.

Police tracked the Audi sedan to the Federal and Hume Highways, where it was stopped with the assistance of NSW Police.

Inside the vehicle, fuel-soaked clothing items that matched clothing worn by the accused offenders, lighters and face coverings were allegedly discovered.

The three male occupants were subsequently arrested.

They faced NSW courts on Saturday (25 July 2026) so they could be extradited to the ACT. All three were transported back to Canberra that afternoon and evening.

One of the three teenagers, 18-year-old Tuakihekofe Palavi Manapuna from Lethbridge Park, briefly faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Monday (27 July).

He did not apply for bail, and Magistrate James Stewart formally refused it.

“Look after yourself, okay,” he told Mr Manapuna.

Mr Manapuna will next face court on 17 August for a mention. No pleas were entered.

Two other teenagers, both 17 years old and from NSW, have been charged with arson and acts endangering life (throwing an inflammable substance).

They faced the ACT Children’s Court today and cannot be named due to their ages.

In their statement, ACT Policing said their investigation into the alleged arson remains ongoing.

“The Giralang residence has been the target of previous arson incidents and enquiries in relation to any linkages between these incidents are occurring,” the spokesperson said.

Anyone with any information about these alleged incidents is urged to contact Crime Stoppers ACT or call 1800 333 000. Quote 8452176.

Information can be provided anonymously.

canberra.title: Ombudsman warns ATO over bias in tax process
canberra.snippet: Bias in tax administration has again come to light, with the Tax Ombudsman giving the ATO quite a rebuke. In its just-published report of...
canberra.content:
The Tax Ombudsman says unchecked bias in the ATO can badly affect someone’s livelihood. Photo: LPETTET.

Bias in tax administration has again come to light, with the Tax Ombudsman giving the ATO quite a rebuke.

In its just-published report of a review of the system, the Tax Ombudsman has warned that unchecked bias in tax administration can have serious consequences for taxpayers.

It has found the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) should do more to manage the risk.

The review was initiated after an investigation into historical allegations of ATO maladministration involving bias and prejudice.

It examined whether the ATO’s current processes, guidance and training prevented bias or prejudice from influencing its decisions, particularly where they can significantly affect a person’s livelihood.

A review of the ATO’s management of a complex and long-running case, along with a follow-up review, considered broader systemic risks of bias or prejudice in the ATO’s decision-making and inappropriate disclosures of taxpayer information.

It examined whether the failings identified in the historic case could occur now and whether the ATO’s current controls were effective in mitigating such risks.

Tax Ombudsman Ruth Owen said the review found that while the ATO had strengthened its controls to improve decision-making in response to weaknesses identified 10 to 15 years ago, there remains plenty of room for improvement.

“The ATO has improved how it makes decisions about taxpayers in recent years; however, this review shows there’s more to be done, particularly by explicitly recognising bias as a risk and strengthening controls so they are embedded in the ATO’s everyday processes,” she said.

“Guarding against bias is not a set-and-forget exercise. It requires ongoing vigilance, regular review, and a willingness to continually challenge assumptions as circumstances, data, and risks evolve.

“The community expects the ATO to act impartially, lawfully, objectively and without bias or prejudice, regardless of a taxpayer’s past behaviour or history.

“The ATO’s decisions must always be based on evidence, applied fairly and regularly checked against the risk of bias.”

Ms Owen said she was also concerned about the ATO breaking its own rules or processes because it believes it is acting in the public interest.

She said she had heard concerns from taxpayers and tax professionals that once a taxpayer is labelled as “bad” it is difficult for them to remove that label, and this could ultimately undermine public confidence in the ATO’s impartiality.

The review found some of the ATO’s processes were not designed to counter bias, meaning staff were not explicitly prompted to consider the risk of bias in their decision-making and to retain an open mind in considering the facts.

Bias and prejudicial conduct can impact tax administration in many ways, she said. For example, officers may depart from procedures or the law to reach a predetermined outcome because they believe they are acting in a “noble cause”.

Alternatively, investigators can give too much weight to past compliance behaviours instead of looking at current evidence with fresh eyes.

“While bias exists in all organisations, the risk is heightened in teams regularly dealing with non-compliance or suspected wrongdoing,” Ms Owen said.

“Strong bias controls are not about second-guessing ATO officers; they are about protecting people from avoidable harm, supporting good decision-making and maintaining public confidence in the tax system.”

The review has made two recommendations to the ATO:

  • Assure itself and the community that its controls against bias and prejudice in compliance and enforcement actions and decision-making are working effectively, and
  • Develop and implement a plan to address identified gaps in bias controls, including strengthening explicit bias checks, training, assurance guidance, data and monitoring, and the language used in disclosures.

Given the nature of the topic that was reviewed and the ombudsman’s specific focus on the ATO’s internal controls, it did not seek broad public input for the review. Instead, it undertook targeted consultation with selected tax professionals and associations.

The ATO has accepted both recommendations.

“The ATO welcomes this report and its contribution to maintaining community confidence in fair, objective and evidence-based tax administration,” Second Commissioner of Taxation, Jeremy Hirschhorn, said in the ATO’s response.

“We recognise that public trust in the tax and superannuation systems depends on confidence that ATO decisions are made impartially, consistently and in accordance with the law.

“We are pleased that the review recognises the significant controls already in place within the ATO to support objective decision-making and manage bias.

“We welcome the opportunity to build on those foundations and reinforce community confidence in the integrity of our decisions and actions. The ATO agrees with both recommendations in the report.”

The Tax Ombudsman will monitor the ATO’s progress in responding to her recommendations.

canberra.title: Government building to stay shut after more asbestos found
canberra.snippet: A government building in the city will remain closed until further notice after asbestos was found in other areas beyond the plant room w...
canberra.content:
27 July 2026

Join the conversation

2

The contractor was working on how to safely remediate the identified contamination and address the source of the issue. Photo: ACT Government.

A government building in the city will remain closed until further notice after asbestos was found in other areas beyond the plant room where it was originally detected.

The find by the contractor means the clean-up will be larger and take longer than originally thought, with a reopening date unknown.

The building at 1 Moore Street was shut down earlier this month after the identification of an asbestos-containing material (ACM). It was slated to reopen on 7 August, but on expert advice this was no longer possible.

The landlord, Infrastructure Canberra, said ongoing investigations had identified ACM in other non-occupied areas of the building.

Testing had not identified ACM in occupied areas of the building under normal operating conditions, but the new ACM found meant that a comprehensive removal, cleaning and remediation program was required across the building.

A specialist asbestos remediation contractor had been appointed and begun work on site.

Infrastructure Canberra said that once the contractor had completed detailed planning and the full scope and schedule of works was confirmed, an updated timeframe for the building’s reopening would be provided.

“We anticipate a revised reopening date will become clearer within the next three weeks, and if advice can be provided sooner we are committed to doing so,” Infrastructure Canberra said.

The contractor was working on how to safely remediate the identified contamination and address the source of the issue.

The remediation program would include ACM removal where required, detailed cleaning activities, validation testing and other works necessary to support the safe reoccupation of the building.

“Remediation will be undertaken in a staged and methodical manner, with testing and verification carried out throughout the process to confirm the effectiveness of the works and inform subsequent stages of remediation,” Infrastructure Canberra said.

Infrastructure Canberra said it would continue to work closely with tenant agencies and service providers to support business continuity and minimise disruption while remediation works were underway.

“The health and safety of building occupants remains our highest priority,” it said.

“Decisions regarding access to and reoccupation of 1 Moore Street will continue to be guided by specialist expert advice and the outcomes of remediation and verification activities.”

The building is home to the City Community Health Centre, other health services, the CanTEST pill-testing facility, and the Canberra Innovation Network (CBRIN).

Health service appointments have been rescheduled at other locations

CanTest is now running its full operations at the YWCA building, 71 Northbourne Avenue in the city, on level 5 on Thursday from 3 pm to 6 pm and Friday from 6 pm to 9 pm.

The CBRIN team continues to operate remotely and arrange alternative spaces for companies and others to use.

australia.title: Secret tape recordings and ‘sham’ payments: the Liberals’ internal ideological war laid bare
australia.snippet: The NSW anti-corruption watchdog has begun a public inquiry into allegations of branch stacking, illegal donations, and interference with...
australia.content:
If you ever thought branch stacking was a harmless game played by young, ambitious political operatives seeking to advance within the party, think again.

On Monday, on the first day of the corruption watchdog’s inquiry into operation Rosny, an investigation into allegations of “possible offences under the Electoral Funding Act”, we heard boasts on secret tape recordings from a developer that he had “my hands on the state government” and he had “fucked” the career of a state politician by “taking his seat”. As for the state’s building commissioner, David Chandler, who was a thorn in the developer’s side, he was going to “fuck him sideways”.

In another call, in September 2021, the developer, Jean Nassif, reflects on the “fucking bitch”, the then premier Gladys Berejiklian. “Mate, we thought we’re gonna change her,” he says to the other person on the call, Charles Perrottet.

The opening address of counsel assisting the New South Wales Independent Commission of Inquiry, Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC laid out the allegations in horrifying detail. She said that Nassif, now a fugitive in Lebanon, had used his millions to engage the services of a group of Liberal operatives, known as the Reformers, as consultants.

These young men, Dwyer alleges, ran a major branch stacking operation that was designed to take over the Liberal party and promote their conservative agenda, while at the same time using their influence to deliver the outcomes their benefactor sought.

It was not just idle boasting by Nassif. Soon after that taped call, he got what he wanted: the Baulkham Hills MP, David Elliott, lost his preselection. Kevin Anderson, the minister responsible for the building commissioner, was replaced and Chandler, under enormous pressure, resigned.

The Reformers, Icac heard, included two of the former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet’s brothers – Jean-Claude and Charles – as well as the principals of two public relations firms, Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood.

Dwyer alleges Ellis and Greenwood took consultancy payments over a period of three years between 2019 and 2022, from Nassif and others.

These were “sham” payments, she says, and no real work was provided for these payments.

Instead the money was, she alleges, an illegal donation to the Reformers, and the consultancies an elaborate scheme to avoid either caps on the amount of donations or to funnel donations from banned donors – such as developers and those from the liquor and gaming industry – or both.

The alleged amounts are staggering: $2m from Nassif, more than $250,000 from the Catholic Schools Association and $125,000 from lawyer turned publican Michael O’Hara, who also happens to be the former law partner of right-wing Liberal powerbroker and upper house MP, Damien Tudehope. Tudehope stood down from the frontbench after being called as a witness to the inquiry.

Dwyer also gave hints of the evidence the Icac might have: a huge trove of “encrypted messages” between the young men who are central to this investigation. It appears they are now decrypted.

Icac also has evidence of the fundraisers the Reformers held, at which high-profile members of the Liberal party and others, including Tudehope, Tony Abbott and Alan Jones, were speakers.

Dwyer stressed that what she has outlined are at this stage allegations, not evidence, and that it was for the Icac commissioner, Fabian Gleeson SC, to decide the nature of the payments and crucially, the intentions of the key actors.

She urged the public not to get despondent at the sheer scale and breadth of the alleged schemes.

But it will be hard for those who follow this inquiry not to feel very alarmed about the state of our democracy, and what it may imply about how both major parties select candidates and determine policy and priorities.

For the first time we are seeing the internal ideological war within the Liberal party laid bare.

Dwyer read from a dossier – the Reformers’ sales pitch- which was prepared to recruit donors and members.

It says they planned to recruit 5,000 members by 2022 and take back the NSW Liberal party for conservatives, aimed to deliver 75% of the seats in the NSW parliament to conservatives by 2023, and sought control over the Liberal party’s peak body, the NSW state executive.

Their agenda? More conservative policies on same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia.

But branch stacking requires significant funds, both to pay the fees of the members who are stacked and the time of the stackers. They needed cash – and that meant finding covert donations.

“Money in politics as in other spheres has the potential to corrupt,” Dwyer told the inquiry.

Just how she alleges it corrupted in NSW remains to be seen. But her opening address hinted that it may have infected decisions on developments, Liberal party preselections, and led to attempts to unseat the building commissioner, David Chandler, to name a few.

Before the ALP gets too smug about the tsunami of horrible news that is going to engulf the NSW Liberals, there is a third allegation of blackmail and corrupt conduct involving Labor councillors at Strathfield council.

They appear to have caught, on the phone taps uncovered during operation Rosny, allegedly planning blackmail of a fellow councillor.

For all major political parties facing an ascendant One Nation, who markets itself as anti-establishment, this inquiry could not have come at a worse time.

Trust in our major parties is low. It’s about to get much lower.

australia.title: So how do you get access to the Qantas chairman’s lounge? Alan Joyce has some tips
australia.snippet: In his memoir the former Qantas chief executive denies using the lounge as a tool to influence politicians Get our breaking news email , ...
australia.content:
Judges, politicians, newspaper editors and big spenders: Alan Joyce, the former Qantas chief executive, has revealed how the airline admits members to its private chairman’s lounge.

In his memoir, released on Tuesday, Joyce denies using the lounge as a tool to influence politicians and claims famous Australians “begged” to be granted access to “arguably the most exclusive club in the country”.

The Irish-born Joyce was one of the airline’s longest-serving heads, leading the company from 2008 until his resignation in 2023.

He has previously described the lounge as a “commercial arrangement”, but the comments in his memoir, Riding the Jet Stream, provide his most expansive explanation of how access to the luxury private zones in Australia’s major airports operates.

Joyce writes that neither he nor the Qantas chair personally handled invitations to the lounge and had only occasional input.

Membership of the “invitation-only” club was approved by a small group of senior executives, he says.

The “core” membership included “federal politicians, most state politicians, high court and federal judges, editors of national newspapers, a few journalists, and high-profile celebrities”.

Companies that spent about $1m each year on Qantas flights “likely” received one lounge membership each, which could be rotated between executives, Joyce writes.

In 2023 the company told a Senate inquiry it also extended invitations to secretaries and deputy secretaries of federal departments, agency chairs, chief executives and commissioners.

Qantas has been contacted for comment.

‘You cannot buy your way in’

In his book, Joyce writes that the company once had to rescind memberships after numbers grew “out of control”, due to “inconsistent oversight”, though he does not specify when that occurred.

Qantas also maintained control of membership by requiring “high standards of conduct”, he writes. Joyce gives the example of Jacqui Lambie, who was banned from the airline for six months after a “rant” in the Melbourne chairman’s lounge, for which she apologised.

Membership feels “elite” and discreet due to the exclusivity, rather than the perks, Joyce writes.

“You cannot buy your way in, and no amount of frequent-flyer points will get you a spot,” he writes.

Free, on-demand fine food and alcohol and comfortable facilities are available at the private lounges. Membership also gives customers free seat selection and priority for customer service, airport check-in and security, baggage handling and upgrade requests, according to the Qantas website.

A number of politicians have handed back their membership of the lounge in recent years.

In his memoir, Joyce denies claims that Qantas exercised influence through lounge membership, describing it as “the wildest assertion”.

“If that were true, Qantas would never have lost a case in the High Court or Federal Court – yet we did,” Joyce writes.

He writes that the lounge was a relationship tool, not a lever of control.

The memoir also contains Joyce’s first public comments on claims he acceded to Anthony Albanese’s requests for free upgrades on Qantas flights, which the prime minister denied in 2024.

“I have no recollection of ever receiving a call from the Prime Minister or his staff requesting an upgrade,” Joyce writes.

Joyce says his standard practice for such requests, which “politicians from all major parties” had made, would have been to tell his personal assistant to arrange the upgrade.

But Joyce says he never asked his assistant nor was there any record of him authorising such an upgrade for Albanese.

“It’s bunkum, but nothing grabs a voter’s attention quite like suggesting a pollie has their nose in the proverbial trough,” he writes.

australia.title: Pauline Hanson and Malcolm Roberts deride family law system, calling DV a ‘weapon’ and court a ‘slaughterhouse’
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Resurfaced comments by the One Nation leader underline her criticism of paid family violence leave and domestic violence suppo...
australia.content:
Pauline Hanson told a podcast last year she believed “your employer should not be responsible” for providing paid domestic violence leave, while her colleague Malcolm Roberts recently referred to the family court as the “slaughterhouse of the nation”, in the latest One Nation comments critical of the family law system to emerge.

Hanson claimed on a 2021 podcast that domestic violence was being “used as a weapon” in court proceedings, and criticised domestic violence groups for focusing on support for women.

“I feel for the children, I feel for the parents and I’m sick of these feminists who are trying to take over this whole thing and who are actually driving their own agenda. I’m sick and tired of hearing that men are the only perpetrators and they’re denied the right to see their children,” Hanson told the Dad Talk Today podcast in 2021.

Hanson’s past comments on domestic violence have drawn renewed scrutiny after a 4BC radio interview last week in which she said family violence was “wrong” but “it’s also a two-way street”.

In an interview with the Broken Fathers podcast last year, Hanson described paid leave for those experiencing family and domestic violence as “ridiculous”, calling it “domestic violence holiday leave”. She also suggested domestic violence was taking police away from “real crime” and called for the family law system to be “wound back”.

Hanson later claimed her 4BC comments had been taken “out of context” and denied she had downplayed domestic violence.

But the newly unearthed comments show the full breadth of One Nation’s criticism of the family law system.

In an interview with Hanson for a podcast titled Unemployable Media in January 2025, during a discussion about challenges facing business owners, the podcast host brought up the issue of domestic violence leave.

“Nobody in Australia would say domestic violence isn’t a horrible thing, but you’ve got 10 days,” the host began saying, before Hanson interjected.

“It should not be tied up in your employment. Your employer should not be responsible,” Hanson said.

The federal Labor government in 2022 legislated for 10 days of paid family and domestic violence leave annually as a workplace entitlement in the National Employment Standards, upgrading the previous five days’ unpaid leave. The cost is borne by employers.

Some businesses raised concerns when the change was legislated, but the social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, said only “a tiny number of people” used the leave.

“But they use it to get medical help, report to police, move to a safer home or go to court”.

The ACTU president, Michele O’Neil, said the scheme was “an essential lifeline available to workers facing some horrifically dangerous situations”.

In the 2021 interview, the One Nation leader criticised “feminist” groups in the domestic violence system.

“You have the domestic violence organisations, they’re getting millions of dollars in funding for it. You’ve got these refuges – and I can see that a woman needs to be protected if they don’t have a house to actually go to with the kids, a safe place to go … but you’ve got to offer the same to a man. You can’t just look after women,” Hanson said.

Later in the interview Hanson claimed domestic violence was “used as a weapon” in court.

“Domestic violence here is, the person can go in and say ‘I’m in fear’ and that can be domestic violence. If you text your partner a number of times ‘I want to see my child’, that’s harassment, that can be domestic violence. If you say ‘honey, sorry why’d you buy another pair of shoes? We’ve got the rent to pay’, that’s domestic violence.”

Roberts, whose advocacy of conspiracy theories has come under scrutiny, also criticised the family court system in a May interview with the rightwing podcast Cafe Locked Out.

“The family law court, a friend of mine describes the family law system as the slaughterhouse of the nation and he’s right,” Roberts said.

“It’s set up to divide. It’s set up to make money for lawyers. It’s set up to smash the family.”

One Nation and Hanson’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

australia.title: Jacinta Allan could face a leadership spill today – here’s what happens next
australia.snippet: Victoria could face weeks of instability if a contest for the leadership of the Labor party goes ahead Who is Ben Carroll, the man who wa...
australia.content:
Urgent talks are being held in the hope of averting a leadership showdown between Jacinta Allan and her deputy, Ben Carroll, that could plunge Victoria’s Labor government into weeks of political turmoil.

The premier and Carroll have publicly declared they would stand in a leadership ballot – expected to be held when caucus meets for the first time since the winter break on Tuesday.

This is despite Allan being told by a cross-factional delegation of ministers and factional leaders on Monday that she did not have the support of the majority of caucus and being urged to step down.

If no compromise is reached, the contest could trigger up to six weeks of instability.

Here’s what we know about how the leadership ballot would work and what could happen next.

world.title: Uganda begins emergency food handouts after 19 die from hunger
world.snippet: Government move follows months of drought and crop failures in Karamoja, with 1.5m people facing malnutrition Uganda has launched emergen...
world.content:
Uganda has launched emergency food relief distribution after at least 19 deaths from hunger were reported in an area of prolonged drought in the east of the country.

A crisis has been building in the Karamoja region of Uganda as crops have failed without the season’s expected rains, leaving the region’s 1.5 million people facing acute food shortages and rising malnutrition.

The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (Fews Net), a global mapping network designed to raise the alert on food security, reported the situation had deteriorated to a crisis across Karamoja.

In the first large-scale operation of its kind organised by the Ugandan government after the funding void left by aid cuts, authorities announced plans to distribute 9,400 tonnes of relief food over the next two months. The supplies were procured using a 45bn-shilling (£9m) emergency funding allocation, approved by parliament.

Sam Engola, minister for disaster preparedness and refugees, launched the aid distribution efforts at a primary school in Lodiko sub-county in Kaabong district on Wednesday.

“The president does not want to hear of anyone in Karamoja dying of hunger. I am here to supervise the distribution of this food to the end. I will ensure that everyone receives food. No one will be left behind,” Engola said.

Karamoja is experiencing its most severe dry spell in years. Farmers have lost crops since the last meaningful rainfall was recorded in April – the beginning of the planting season.

Angelina Nakiru, a 21-year-old mother of two in Rupa, about 5 miles from Moroto town in Karamoja, said she was struggling to feed her children after all her crops failed. Now she goes early each morning to join other women at a small-scale grinding mill where machines are used to crush rock into powder to wash out gold-bearing ore. The pay is meagre.

“The work is dusty and exhausting, but it is the only way I can earn money to buy a cup of maize and beans to feed the children,” Nakiru said.

“If I don’t, the children will sleep hungry. Other days when I fail to get the meagre income from the mill, we go to bed on empty stomachs,” she said.

“The situation is terrible. People are starving and dying due to hunger. The government must come to the rescue of the people.”

Health facilities report treating hundreds of children for severe malnutrition. A nutrition report published in June found nearly half of the population in Karamoja’s Kaabong and Kotido districts in a crisis situation.

Experts attribute the region’s recurring food insecurity and vulnerability to climate crisis shocks, environmental degradation such as deforestation and overgrazing, as well as poverty and low agricultural productivity.

In 2022, a devastating hunger crisis claimed more than 2,200 lives, according to figures from Uganda’s human rights commission body.

While emergency food aid is expected to provide short-term relief, the government said it remained committed to implementing long-term remedial measures with the recently approved Karamoja regional development plan, which is intended to strengthen communities’ resilience to drought.

John Baptist Lokii, minister for Karamoja, said: “The government will provide drought-resistant, disease-resistant and early-maturing seeds ahead of the next planting season.”

Agnes Kirabo, executive director of Uganda’s Food Rights Alliance (FRA), said the government was taking the lead on distribution as a necessity as much as a policy choice as the landscape of humanitarian aid had changed dramatically.

Following significant funding cuts, most notably from USAID, which previously had an annual budget of about $42.8bn (£32.bn), agencies such as the World Food Programme (WFP) have been forced to drastically scale back their aid.

In Uganda, the WFP has phased out food assistance for 63% of the refugee population, cutting off more than 1 million people from aid, and reducing rations to just 663,000 recipients.

“This transition should not be viewed solely as a reaction to aid cuts, but also as a positive shift towards nationally owned, sustainable development. Government leadership is a constructive move, provided it is part of a long-term strategy to establish durable national systems,” said Kirabo.

“Emergency food distribution is a life-saving measure, not a permanent solution. To break this cycle, we must address the root causes of food insecurity through structural reforms.”

The FRA, Kirabo said, wanted access to food to be made a fundamental human right and the government to turn its attention to water infrastructure and climate resilience. “Karamoja possesses adequate rainfall and water routes to achieve food self-sufficiency, but requires the political will to strategically invest in water infrastructure for production,” she said.

“Ultimately, the Karamoja hunger crisis is a governance crisis. The government’s leadership in this emergency is welcome, but it must be matched by the political will to implement the systemic changes required to permanently protect the people of Karamoja and Uganda from predictable, preventable hunger.”

world.title: Two Russian men jailed in Angola for terrorism and spying
world.snippet: The men were convicted over alleged plan to stage coup and organise deadly demonstrations over fuel prices last year Two Russian men have...
world.content:
Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year.

Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities.

From 28-30 July 2025, a minibus taxi strike over fuel price hikes descended into riots and looting, in which 22 people were killed and more than 1,600 arrested according to official figures.

Angola’s security forces were accused of firing live ammunition at protesters; the government said its “progressive” use of force was justified. Human Rights Watch had previously said Angola employed “excessive force” when it used rubber bullets and teargas to break up a peaceful protest against rising fuel prices on 12 July 2025.

Angolan prosecutors said Lakshtanov and Ratchin wanted to influence next year’s presidential elections, including by funding Angola’s largest opposition party, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), or by forcing a leadership change within the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), which has ruled the country since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Prosecutors also claimed the men were linked to Africa Politology, a Russian disinformation and propaganda network that emerged from the Wagner mercenary group.

Africa Politology was taken over by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) after the death of the Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2023, according to an investigation by media outlets including Forbidden Stories. Wagner was rebranded as Africa Corps and absorbed by Russia’s military.

Angola, whose economy is highly dependent on oil exports, has historically been close with Russia. During the cold war years of Angola’s 1975-2002 civil war, the Soviet Union and Cuba supported the MPLA, while the US and apartheid South Africa backed its opponents, including UNITA. However, Angola’s president, João Lourenço, has improved relations with the US and Europe since taking power in 2017.

In the last decade, Russia has increased its presence in Africa. The Wagner group and then Africa Corps have provided security for the Central African Republic’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, since 2017.

In 2021, Wagner forces arrived in Mali to support the military junta. Africa Corps also backs the military regimes in neighbouring Niger and Burkina Faso. Since 2023, Russian troops have also been deployed in Equatorial Guinea, Libya and Sudan, according to a US Congress report.

Madagascar’s president, Michael Randrianirina, has also boosted ties with Russia since taking power in a coup in October 2025. There are Russians in his presidential guard and a weekly programme about Madagascar-Russia relations was launched earlier this month on national television.

Two Angolans were also tried alongside the Russians. The sports journalist Carlos Tomé received a two-year suspended prison sentence. Francisco de Oliveira, the secretary-general of UNITA’s youth wing, was acquitted.

Prosecutors have appealed against those sentences, according to the Portuguese news agency Lusa. Lakshtanov and Ratchin have also appealed against their sentences, but will remain in detention while the appeal is processed, according to Lusa.

Russia’s embassy in Angola did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Agence France-Press contributed to this report

world.title: MoD cancels army training in Kenya over powers to prosecute British soldiers
world.snippet: September exercise called off after Kenya raises concerns over funding and jurisdiction for criminal offences The British army has been f...
world.content:
The British army has been forced to cancel training for its troops in Kenya after the Kenyan government refused to ratify a bilateral defence agreement.

While the UK government wanted to renew the existing agreement, Kenyan lawmakers had sought changes to give local authorities greater powers to hold British soldiers accountable for any offences committed in the country.

According to the Kenyan news outlet the Daily Nation, the dispute centres on which cases Kenya will retain primary jurisdiction over, while the amount of money Britain pays Kenya to host the training camp has also been a sticking point.

The chair of the Kenyan national assembly’s defence, intelligence and foreign relations committee, Nelson Koech, said the two governments were “actively engaging to address these outstanding issues”.

As a result of the Kenyan government’s decision, a planned exercise involving the 1st Battalion the Duke of Lancaster’s Regiment, which was due to begin in September, has been cancelled.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “The UK highly values its relationship with Kenya, which is underpinned by mutual benefit, respect and cooperation. The UK-Kenya Defence Partnership is one of the great strengths of our relationship. Our joint training and operations with the Kenyan Defence Forces are keeping both Kenyan and British people safe.

“It is with regret that the necessary licences required to allow training to take place in Laikipia later this year have not been forthcoming. As a result, the planned training will now be conducted at an alternative location outside Kenya.”

Kenya also benefits from training of its own armed forces at BATUK, the British army base near Nanyuki, and the presence of British troops is valuable for the economy.

The MoD spokesperson added: “We recognise the disappointment this decision will cause for those who would have benefited from the economic activity generated by the exercise.”

They said the UK government remained “committed to our defence partnership with Kenya”, adding that the UK would “continue to engage closely with the Kenyan government to support the resumption of training in-country at the earliest appropriate opportunity”.

However, there has been sustained pressure from Kenyan people opposed to the British army’s continued presence. Last year, a report to the Kenyan parliament into the base alleged human rights violations, environmental destruction and sexual abuse by British soldiers.

The most high-profile case linked to the base is the death of Agnes Wanjiru, in which a British soldier has been charged with murder. Kenya has retained jurisdiction in the case and an extradition hearing is due to take place in November. Robert Purkiss denies the single charge of murder.

Legal proceedings had stalled since Wanjiru’s death in 2012, but advanced under John Healey’s tenure as defence secretary. As shadow defence secretary, he had called on the previous government to do more to progress the case.

Koech said the committee had called for “stronger accountability measures, including jurisdiction over serious offences, enhanced protection for local communities, and implementation of recommendations arising from the BATUK inquiry”.

world.title: Health worker monitored for Ebola in London hospital after working in DRC
world.snippet: UK resident was evacuated from Democratic Republic of the Congo where there is an outbreak of the disease A humanitarian worker is being ...
world.content:
A humanitarian worker is being monitored at a specialist hospital in London after potential exposure to the Ebola virus.

The UK resident was medically evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) where the worker had been treating patients with the disease, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said.

UKHSA said the person was evacuated as a “highly precautionary measure”, adding: “The individual is not currently displaying any symptoms and remains well, but as a precautionary measure they have been evacuated on a flight chartered solely for the evacuation.

“They are now being assessed and monitored in isolation by infectious disease specialists at a London hospital.”

The agency said the incubation period of Ebola ranges from two to 21 days and the individual will be closely monitored and is required to isolate throughout this period.

There are no confirmed cases of Ebola in the UK and the risk to the general public remains low.

Richard Pebody, the director of epidemic and emerging infections at the UKHSA, said: “This individual has been transferred out of an abundance of caution and we’re pleased they remain well.”

Last month, a patient suspected of having the Ebola virus at a Glasgow hospital tested negative.

Precautionary measures were taken after the patient was admitted to the Queen Elizabeth University hospital.

An outbreak of the disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda in May was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the World Health Organization (WHO).

The virus is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected people and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle, pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash, and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.

world.title: Healthy diet too expensive for one in three people globally, UN report finds
world.snippet: Global hunger declined for the third year in a row in 2025 but experts call for action to bring down costs of fruit, vegetables and dairy...
world.content:
One in three people cannot afford to eat a healthy diet, a new report has found, prompting calls for urgent action on food affordability.

There are 2.69 billion people unable to afford a diverse diet that meets their energy and nutrient needs, and it will take “immense” amounts of work to achieve the global target of zero hunger by 2030, the annual report from five UN agencies warned.

Global hunger declined for a third consecutive year in 2025, with 7.8% of people affected, down from 8.1% in 2024. There were also signs that a prolonged upward trend in Africa was coming to a halt.

However, the proportion of people who cannot afford a healthy diet remains “extremely high”, said Maximo Torero, chief economist of the Food and Agriculture Organization, one of the report’s authors.

The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 report calculated the cost of a healthy diet is 4.28 purchasing power parity (PPP) dollars a day. This means that in any given country, a healthy diet costs the amount of local currency with the same buying power that $4.28 has in the US.

“The extreme poverty line is $3PPP per person,” Torero said. “So it’s significantly higher.”

He said government policies had typically focused on subsidising cereals and starchy staples, rather than meat, dairy, fruit and vegetables.

“That means calories, but not a diversity of diet,” he said, highlighting the impact of this on rates of obesity and diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

Figures from the World Health Organization, another of the UN agencies behind the report, show adult obesity rose from 12.1% in 2012 to 16.2% in 2024.

“It’s extremely urgent,” Torero said. “Obesity [among adults] is growing at a very steep level, so we need to now work intensively on trying to minimise those risks and those hidden costs that that substantial increase in obesity will bring.”

He called for investment in infrastructure, research and development. Modelling in the report suggests more efficient supply chains could bring down the costs of meat and dairy as well as fruit and vegetables. New policies to encourage greater consumption of fruit and vegetables could also pay dividends, he suggested, reducing the economic impact of health issues linked to poor diets.

In Africa, 66.6% of the population was unable to afford a healthy diet in 2025, more than double the levels observed in Asia or Latin America and the Caribbean.

Africa is now home to the highest number of hungry people for the first time, with about 309 million, surpassing Asia’s 292 million, the report showed.

The rise is largely driven by higher population growth on the continent, Torero said, with the proportion of the population going hungry actually starting to decrease “for the first time in years”.

“I think this is extremely important, because the numbers are for 2025, where already we have seen a significant reduction in overseas development assistance in the region,” Torero said.

Shipping restrictions in the strait of Hormuz linked to the conflict in the Middle East are likely to hit next year’s figures, he said.

The report is authored by the FAO, WHO, Unicef, the UN World Food Programme and the International Fund for Agricultural Development.
